claims.claim: Known p53-regulated tumor-suppressor lncRNAs were consistently negatively associated with the proliferation/growth-regulating co-essential modules.
claims.source: The meta-analysis indicates known p53-regulated tumor-suppressor lncRNAs (e.g., PICART1 [Cao et al., 2017], LINC00475 [Melo et al., 2016], NEAT1 [Mello et al., 2017], LNCTAM34A/GUARDIN [Hu et al., 2018], and ST7-AS1 [Sheng et al., 2021]) were consistently negatively associated with the proliferation/growth-regulating co-essential modules (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations and reference to Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Elevated levels of known p53-regulated tumor-suppressor lncRNAs upon p53 activation suppress tumorigenesis.
claims.source: Literature evidence suggests that elevated levels of these lncRNAs upon p53 activation suppress tumorigenesis (Cao et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2018; Mello et al., 2017; Melo et al., 2016; Sheng et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The proliferation/growth-linked lncRNAs preferentially regulate proliferation across TCGA cancer types compared to other Hallmark processes.
claims.source: We determined that the proliferation/growth-linked lncRNAs, identified from the cell line-based evaluation data, preferentially regulate proliferation across TCGA cancer types (median = 142) compared to the other Hallmark processes (median range across the Hallmark categories = 15–99) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TCGA data and reference to Figure 2A.

claims.claim: There is significant variation in the number of regulating lncRNAs of the Hallmark processes across the TCGA cancer types.
claims.source: To investigate whether we biased the results by selecting the top 200 co-expressed protein-coding genes, we conducted Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) (Subramanian et al., 2005), considering all the genes that have significant (BH adjusted p<0.001) association with each lncRNA to connect the lncRNA with cancer Hallmark processes. The top five significantly (BH adjusted p<0.05) enriched gene signatures were connected to each lncRNA. Again, significant (p=8.68 × 10–14; ANOVA) variation in the number of regulating lncRNAs of the Hallmark processes across the TCGA cancer types was obtained (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ANOVA statistical test (p=8.68 × 10^-14) and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Proliferation was regulated by a higher number of lncRNAs compared to other Hallmark categories in TCGA cancer types.
claims.source: Importantly, proliferation was regulated by a higher number of lncRNAs (median = 187) compared to the other Hallmark categories (median range across Hallmark categories = 7–135) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the GSEA analysis results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The lncRNAs predicted as potential inducers showed significantly higher positive associations with proliferation genesets across cancer types.
claims.source: We determined that the lncRNAs predicted as potential inducers and suppressors in the CCLE data showed significantly higher positive (5.17 × 10–4; Wilcoxon rank-sum test) and negative (3.19 × 10–3; Wilcoxon rank-sum test) associations, respectively, with proliferation genesets across the cancer types (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Wilcoxon rank-sum test (p=5.17 × 10^-4) and reference to Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The lncRNAs predicted as potential suppressors showed significantly higher negative associations with proliferation genesets across cancer types.
claims.source: We determined that the lncRNAs predicted as potential inducers and suppressors in the CCLE data showed significantly higher positive (5.17 × 10–4; Wilcoxon rank-sum test) and negative (3.19 × 10–3; Wilcoxon rank-sum test) associations, respectively, with proliferation genesets across the cancer types (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Wilcoxon rank-sum test (p=3.19 × 10^-3) and reference to Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Predicted proliferation/growth inducers and suppressors had a significantly distinct distribution of expression alterations in 9 out of 10 cancer types.
claims.source: Predicted proliferation/growth inducers and suppressors had a significantly distinct distribution of expression alterations in 9 out of 10 cancer types (Figure 2C; p<0.05, BH adjusted Wilcoxon rank-sum test; Supplementary file 2a, Figure 2—source data 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical test (BH adjusted Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05) and reference to Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The median fold change of proliferation inducers indicates their coordinated overexpression in all 10 TCGA cancer types.
claims.source: The median fold change of proliferation inducers indicates their coordinated overexpression in all 10 TCGA cancer types, and the suppressors showed coordinated downregulation in 7 cancer types (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The suppressors showed coordinated downregulation in 7 cancer types.
claims.source: The median fold change of proliferation inducers indicates their coordinated overexpression in all 10 TCGA cancer types, and the suppressors showed coordinated downregulation in 7 cancer types (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: 91% of known proliferation-inducing lncRNAs have potentially induced proliferation/growth in a higher number of TCGA cancer types by regulating a higher number of Hallmark proliferation genesets.
claims.source: We also determined that 91% of known proliferation-inducing lncRNAs (highlighted in Figure 1E) have potentially induced proliferation/growth in a higher number of TCGA cancer types by regulating a higher number of Hallmark proliferation genesets (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis results shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Four of five known p53-regulated tumor-suppressor lncRNAs show a negative impact on a higher number of proliferation genesets across TCGA cancer types.
claims.source: Similarly, four of five known p53-regulated tumor-suppressor lncRNAs show a negative impact on a higher number of proliferation genesets across TCGA cancer types (Figures 1E and 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis results shown in Figures 1E and 2D.

claims.claim: 30 uncharacterized or poorly characterized lncRNAs potentially regulate at least five Hallmark proliferation-linked genesets across five or more TCGA cancer types.
claims.source: We determined 30 uncharacterized or poorly characterized lncRNAs that potentially regulate at least five Hallmark proliferation-linked genesets across five or more TCGA cancer types (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis results shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Proliferation/growth-suppressing lncRNAs were preferentially elevated in cells treated by DNA-damaging proliferation inhibitors compared to control.
claims.source: By analyzing seven RNA-seq datasets, we identified the proliferation/growth-regulating lncRNAs altered at least twofold in cells treated by one of the proliferation-inhibiting DNA-damaging stimuli (doxorubicin, 5-fluorouracil, gamma radiation) compared to control (Supplementary file 2b). We determined proliferation/growth-suppressing and -inducing lncRNAs were preferentially elevated and reduced, respectively (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of seven RNA-seq datasets and shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Proliferation/growth-inducing lncRNAs were preferentially reduced in cells treated by DNA-damaging proliferation inhibitors compared to control.
claims.source: By analyzing seven RNA-seq datasets, we identified the proliferation/growth-regulating lncRNAs altered at least twofold in cells treated by one of the proliferation-inhibiting DNA-damaging stimuli (doxorubicin, 5-fluorouracil, gamma radiation) compared to control (Supplementary file 2b). We determined proliferation/growth-suppressing and -inducing lncRNAs were preferentially elevated and reduced, respectively (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of seven RNA-seq datasets and shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Nutlin-treated cells showed a preferential up- and downregulation of the proliferation/growth-suppressing and -inducing lncRNAs, respectively, compared with control cells.
claims.source: Compared with the control cells, Nutlin-treated cells showed a preferential up- and downregulation (at least twofold) of the proliferation/growth-suppressing and -inducing lncRNAs, respectively, similarly to what we observed from the cells treated by the DNA-damaging proliferation inhibitors (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq datasets and shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Reproducible expression patterns were observed in Nutlin-treated single-cell RNA-seq profiles with p53 wild-type cells, but not for cells with mutant p53.
claims.source: Furthermore, we observed reproducible expression patterns in Nutlin-treated single-cell RNA-seq profiles with p53 wild-type cells, but not for cells with mutant p53 (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The identified proliferation/growth-regulating lncRNAs have notable crosstalk with p53-mediated tumor-suppressive pathways.
claims.source: Our results suggest that our identified proliferation/growth-regulating lncRNAs have notable crosstalk with p53-mediated tumor-suppressive pathways.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the results showing differential expression of lncRNAs in response to p53 activation.

claims.claim: The majority (59%) of lncRNAs showed differential expression in only one or two datasets, which supports cell type-specific functions of these lncRNAs.
claims.source: The majority (59%) of lncRNAs showed differential expression in only one or two datasets, which supports cell type-specific functions of these lncRNAs (Liu et al., 2017b; Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1j).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and citation to Liu et al., 2017b.

claims.claim: Less than 5% of the lncRNAs were altered in more than five datasets.
claims.source: We determined that less than 5% of the lncRNAs were altered in more than five datasets (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1j).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Meta-analysis identified 13 consistently upregulated lncRNAs across the RNA-seq datasets, and of them, 8 were identified as the top proliferation/growth suppressors.
claims.source: Conducting RobustRankAggreg-based meta-analysis, we identified 13 consistently upregulated lncRNAs across the RNA-seq datasets, and of them, 8 were identified as the top proliferation/growth suppressors (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1k).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the RobustRankAggreg meta-analysis results shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Meta-analysis identified four consistently downregulated lncRNAs and three of them were identified as the top proliferation/growth inducers.
claims.source: We also identified four consistently downregulated lncRNAs and three of them were identified as the top proliferation/growth inducers (Supplementary file 1l).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the RobustRankAggreg meta-analysis results.

claims.claim: TMPO-AS1 was one of the top proliferation/growth-inducing lncRNAs and had more than twofold downregulation in six RNA-seq datasets.
claims.source: For example, a known pan-cancer onco-lncRNA, TMPO-AS1, was one of the top proliferation/growth-inducing lncRNAs and had more than twofold downregulation in six RNA-seq datasets (Zheng et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis and citation to Zheng et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Among the eight consistently upregulated lncRNAs, three are known p53-regulated tumor suppressors (GUARDIN, PICART1, and LINC00475).
claims.source: Conversely, among the eight consistently upregulated lncRNAs, three are known p53-regulated tumor suppressors (GUARDIN, PICART1, and LINC00475) (Cao et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2018; Melo et al., 2016; Figure 3C), whereas the remaining lncRNAs have not been previously investigated for p53 regulation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cao et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2018; Melo et al., 2016 and reference to Figure 3C.

claims.claim: A significantly higher number of ChIP-seq datasets had p53-binding sites within 10 kilobases from the transcription start site of the 13 consistently upregulated lncRNAs compared with the remaining lncRNAs.
claims.source: We determined that a significantly (p=1.65 × 10–9; Wilcoxon rank-sum test) higher number of ChIP-seq datasets had p53-binding sites within 10 kilobases from the transcription start site of these lncRNAs compared with the remaining lncRNAs (background data) annotated in GENCODE version 27 (Frankish et al., 2019; Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Wilcoxon rank-sum test (p=1.65 × 10^-9) and reference to Figure 3D.

claims.claim: FAM198B-AS1 (PSLR-1) and SEPTIN9-DT (PSLR-2) had consistently elevated expression upon p53 activation across diverse cell types and treatments.
claims.source: The two poorly characterized top proliferation suppressing lncRNAs (PSLRs) FAM198B-AS1 (PSLR-1) and SEPTIN9-DT (PSLR-2) identified in our analysis had consistently elevated expression upon p53 activation across diverse cell types and treatments (more than twofold in at least six RNA-seq datasets; BH adjusted RobustRankAggreg p<5.48 × 10–3) (Figures 2E, 3C and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by meta-analysis results (BH adjusted RobustRankAggreg p<5.48 × 10^-3) and reference to figures.

claims.claim: PSLR-1 and PSLR-2 had p53-binding sites in at least nine ChIP-seq datasets.
claims.source: These two lncRNAs also had p53-binding sites in at least nine ChIP-seq datasets (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Following exposure to p53-activating stimuli, levels of PSLR-1 and PSLR-2 were significantly increased compared to vehicle control-treated cells in A549 and H460 LUAD cell lines.
claims.source: Following exposure to any of the four p53-activating stimuli, levels of these two lncRNAs were significantly increased compared to vehicle control-treated cells (Figure 3F, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Both PSLR-1 and PSLR-2 were significantly reduced in LUAD patient samples compared to normal lung tissue.
claims.source: Both lncRNAs were significantly (p<1.23 × 10–7; t-test) reduced in LUAD patient samples compared to normal lung tissue, indicating suppression of their functions during tumorigenesis (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from patient samples (t-test, p<1.23 × 10^-7) shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Elevated expression of PSLR-1 or PSLR-2 results in significantly higher expression of genes that had significant positive associations with the lncRNAs in TCGA LUAD patient cohort compared with genes that had significant negative associations.
claims.source: From the lncRNA perturbation data, we determined that elevated expression of either of the two lncRNAs results in significantly (p<7.9 × 10–12; Wilcoxon rank-sum test) higher expression of those genes that had significant (BH adjusted regression p<0.001) positive associations with the lncRNAs in the TCGA LUAD patient cohort compared with the genes that had significant negative associations (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data from lncRNA overexpression experiments (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<7.9 × 10^-12) shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: With elevated expression of each lncRNA in A549 cells, tumor-suppressor genes and oncogenes were preferentially elevated and suppressed, respectively.
claims.source: With elevated expression of each lncRNA in A549 cells, the tumor-suppressor genes and the oncogenes were preferentially elevated and suppressed, respectively (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The distribution of expression changes of tumor-suppressor genes and oncogenes was significantly distinct with elevated PSLR expression.
claims.source: Moreover, the distribution of their expression changes was significantly distinct (p<5.6 × 10–6; Wilcoxon rank-sum test), indicating these lncRNAs act as negative regulators of lung tumorigenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical test (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<5.6 × 10^-6).

claims.claim: The p53 pathway was consistently ranked as the top among the significantly upregulated Hallmark genesets in A549 cells with elevated levels of PSLR-1 and PSLR-2.
claims.source: The p53 pathway was consistently ranked as the top among the significantly (FDR < 0.05) upregulated Hallmark genesets in A549 cells with elevated levels of the two lncRNAs (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA results (FDR < 0.05) shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Proliferation-linked Hallmark genesets (E2F targets, G2M checkpoint, mitotic spindle, and MYC targets V1 and V2) were consistently ranked among the top significantly downregulated pathways/genesets with elevated PSLR expression.
claims.source: In contrast, the proliferation-linked Hallmark genesets (E2F targets, G2M checkpoint, mitotic spindle, and MYC targets V1 and V2) were also consistently ranked among the top significantly (FDR < 0.05) downregulated pathways/genesets, indicating they were negatively impacted with the overexpression of the two lncRNAs (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA results (FDR < 0.05) shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Increased PSLR-1 or -2 expression showed E2F4 and FOXM1 were the most enriched transcriptional regulators for the downregulated genes.
claims.source: Increased PSLR-1 or -2 expression showed E2F4 and FOXM1 were the most enriched transcriptional regulators for the downregulated genes, and p53 was the top transcriptional regulator for the upregulated genes (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Enrichr analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: p53 was the top transcriptional regulator for the upregulated genes with increased PSLR expression.
claims.source: Increased PSLR-1 or -2 expression showed E2F4 and FOXM1 were the most enriched transcriptional regulators for the downregulated genes, and p53 was the top transcriptional regulator for the upregulated genes (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Enrichr analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: CHR (cell cycle genes homology region) was consistently among the top enriched motifs for both PSLR-1 and -2 in promoters of downregulated genes.
claims.source: We determined that cell cycle genes homology region (CHR), a DNA element present in promoters of many cell cycle genes bound by E2F4 and/or FOXM1-containing protein complexes (Chen et al., 2013), was consistently among the top enriched motifs for both PSLR-1 and -2 (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by HOMER motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4F and citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claims.claim: G2/M cell cycle genes with CHR sites are activated by a FOXM1-containing protein complex.
claims.source: Recent reports indicate that G2/M cell cycle genes with CHR sites are activated by a FOXM1-containing protein complex (Chen et al., 2013; Sadasivam et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013 and Sadasivam et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Expression of PSLR-1 or PSLR-2 resulted in significantly decreased LUAD cell growth compared to cells with empty vector.
claims.source: Expression of each lncRNA resulted in significantly decreased LUAD cell growth compared to cells with empty vector (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by MTT assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Overexpression of MALAT1 increased LUAD cell growth.
claims.source: Serving as an lncRNA control, we overexpressed MALAT1, a pro-proliferative lncRNA (Tripathi et al., 2013), which increased LUAD cell growth (Figure 5A, Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by MTT assay data shown in Figure 5A and citation to Tripathi et al., 2013.

claims.claim: There was a decrease in the number of colonies formed from cells expressing PSLR-1 or PSLR-2 compared to cells with an empty vector or MALAT1.
claims.source: Additionally, there was a decrease in the number of colonies formed from cells expressing PSLR-1 or PSLR-2 compared to cells with an empty vector or MALAT1 (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: There was a significant decrease in live cell numbers with expression of PSLR-1 or PSLR-2 without changes in cell viability.
claims.source: Because there was a significant decrease in live cell numbers with expression of these lncRNAs (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 3) without changes in cell viability (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), we evaluated cell cycle.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Trypan Blue exclusion data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Expression of PSLR-1 or PSLR-2 resulted in increased numbers of cells in the G2/M phase of the cell cycle.
claims.source: Expression of PSLR-1 or PSLR-2 resulted in increased numbers of cells in the G2/M phase of the cell cycle (Figure 5D, Figure 5—source data 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: There was an analogous percentage of cells with phospho-histone H3 in cells expressing any of the lncRNAs or vector control, indicating the cells were arresting in G2 and not M.
claims.source: To discriminate between cells in G2 and M phases, we evaluated phospho-histone H3, a marker of mitosis (Hans and Dimitrov, 2001). There was an analogous percentage of cells with phospho-histone H3 in cells expressing any of the lncRNAs or vector control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating the cells were arresting in G2 and not M.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by phospho-histone H3 staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and citation to Hans and Dimitrov, 2001.

claims.claim: There was reduced expression of nine G2 regulatory genes with elevated PSLR levels.
claims.source: There was reduced expression of nine genes (blue squares; median fold change 7.67; median FDR = 2.27 × 10–91) and increased expression of three genes (red squares; median fold change 7.32; median FDR = 4.66 × 10–52) with elevated PSLR levels, which would result in cells arresting in the G2-phase of the cell cycle (Figure 6A).

results.result: The manuscript establishes the background context for lncRNA research in cancer, noting that >100,000 lncRNAs exist in the human genome, they function as critical modulators of gene expression, their expression is altered in cancer, but only a small fraction have been functionally characterized, particularly regarding their roles in cell proliferation/growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 are well-supported by appropriate citations to the literature (Zhao et al., 2021; Statello et al., 2021; Bao et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2017b; Ning et al., 2016; Schmitt and Chang, 2016) and represent established knowledge in the field. These background claims provide appropriate context for the study.

results.result: The manuscript establishes that while genome-scale CRISPR-Cas9 screens have identified >1800 essential genes across >700 cancer cell lines, lncRNA loss-of-function screens have lagged significantly behind, with only seven cell lines screened for growth/survival modulating lncRNA loci and nine lncRNAs identified in keratinocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 are supported by appropriate citations (Blomen et al., 2015; Hart et al., 2015; Tsherniak et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2017a; Cai et al., 2020) and establish the gap in knowledge that motivates the current study. The contrast between protein-coding gene screens and lncRNA screens is well-documented.

results.result: The manuscript establishes that over 5000 co-essential gene complexes/modules have been identified from CRISPR screens, these modules recapitulate known pathways with oncogenic functions, and functionally related genes are highly enriched in co-essential modules.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C13 are supported by citation to Wainberg et al., 2021 and provide the conceptual foundation for the hypothesis that mapping lncRNAs to co-essential modules can predict lncRNA functions. This represents appropriate use of prior work to motivate the current approach.

results.result: The study developed a multivariate regression model to estimate lncRNA-gene co-expression networks while accounting for noise from DNA methylation and copy number alterations, and applied this model to 807 CCLE cancer cell lines and 3017 patient samples across 10 TCGA cancer types.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C19 are supported by appropriate citations (Jacobsen et al., 2013; Mitra et al., 2020; Mitra et al., 2017; Ghandi et al., 2019; Hoadley et al., 2018) and references to Figure 1A and supplements. The methodological approach is clearly described and builds on established methods for controlling confounding factors in gene regulatory networks.

results.result: From CCLE-based lncRNA-gene networks, the study identified 1049 (6.6%) lncRNAs with significantly enriched associations with pan-cancer essential genes, including 549 with positive associations and 500 with negative associations.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22 are supported by rigorous statistical analysis (hypergeometric test with BH adjusted p<10^-10) and reference to Figure 1A. The stringent significance cutoff and clear reporting of numbers provide confidence in these findings. The statistical approach is appropriate for identifying enriched associations.

results.result: The co-essential modules were preferentially enriched with proliferation/growth-regulating genesets compared to other pathways, and 1027 lncRNAs potentially regulate 78 proliferation/growth-linked co-essential modules, with modules being positively or negatively impacted by inducing or suppressing lncRNAs, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 are supported by statistical testing (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p=2.06×10^-4) and references to Figure 1B, 1C, and supplements. The preferential enrichment of proliferation pathways validates the approach and the directional associations provide mechanistic insight. The data presentation in figures supports these claims.

results.result: Meta-analysis using RobustRankAggreg identified 123 proliferation/growth-inducing lncRNAs and 252 suppressing lncRNAs, with over 66% of identified lncRNAs not previously studied in cancer and another 10% poorly characterized.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C29 are supported by the RobustRankAggreg meta-analysis (BH adjusted p<0.05) and systematic PubMed literature search. The novelty assessment is methodologically sound and demonstrates the discovery potential of the approach. The high percentage of uncharacterized lncRNAs validates the need for this study.

results.result: The computational framework successfully identified known proliferation-inducing lncRNAs as top hits, including multiple SNHG family members, DLEU2, TMPO-AS1, and MIR17HG, validating the predictive accuracy of the approach.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C34 are well-supported by citations to literature (Jin et al., 2019; Zimta et al., 2020; Ghafouri-Fard et al., 2021; Zheng et al., 2021; Mogilyansky and Rigoutsos, 2013) and reference to Figure 1E. The validation against known proliferation-inducing lncRNAs provides strong evidence for the accuracy of the computational predictions.

results.result: The tumor-suppressor p53 negatively impacts essential genes and co-essential modules, and known p53-regulated tumor-suppressor lncRNAs (PICART1, LINC00475, NEAT1, GUARDIN, ST7-AS1) were consistently negatively associated with proliferation/growth-regulating modules, with literature evidence showing their elevated levels suppress tumorigenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 are supported by citation to Wainberg et al., 2021, multiple citations for individual lncRNAs (Cao et al., 2017; Melo et al., 2016; Mello et al., 2017; Hu et al., 2018; Sheng et al., 2021), and reference to Figures 1D and 1E. The validation against known p53-regulated tumor suppressors provides additional evidence for the accuracy of the approach.

results.result: The integrative computational framework consistently prioritizes known proliferation/growth regulators as top hits in evaluation and validation datasets and predicts proliferation/growth dependencies of 289 previously uncharacterized lncRNAs.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C15 are supported by the validation results showing known lncRNAs as top hits (C30-C37) and the computational analysis identifying 289 uncharacterized lncRNAs. The consistency across evaluation and validation datasets strengthens confidence in the predictions.

results.result: In TCGA validation datasets, proliferation/growth-linked lncRNAs preferentially regulate proliferation across cancer types (median=142) compared to other Hallmark processes (median range=15-99), with significant variation in regulating lncRNAs across Hallmark processes confirmed by both top-200 gene and GSEA approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 are supported by ANOVA statistical tests (p=1.96×10^-11 and p=8.68×10^-14) and references to Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The use of two independent analytical approaches (top 200 genes and GSEA) that yield consistent results strengthens confidence in the findings.

results.result: Predicted proliferation/growth inducers and suppressors showed significantly higher positive and negative associations, respectively, with proliferation genesets across TCGA cancer types.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 are supported by Wilcoxon rank-sum tests (p=5.17×10^-4 and p=3.19×10^-3) and reference to Figure 2B. The directional consistency between predictions and validation data provides strong evidence for the accuracy of the classification of lncRNAs as inducers or suppressors.

results.result: Predicted proliferation/growth inducers and suppressors had significantly distinct expression distributions in 9 out of 10 cancer types, with inducers showing coordinated overexpression in all 10 TCGA cancer types and suppressors showing coordinated downregulation in 7 cancer types.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45 are supported by BH adjusted Wilcoxon rank-sum tests (p<0.05) and reference to Figure 2C and Supplementary file 2a. The coordinated expression changes consistent with predicted functions provide strong validation of the computational predictions and suggest selection during tumorigenesis.

results.result: Validation in TCGA data showed that 91% of known proliferation-inducing lncRNAs and 4 of 5 known p53-regulated tumor-suppressor lncRNAs regulate proliferation genesets across multiple cancer types, and identified 30 uncharacterized/poorly characterized lncRNAs that potentially regulate at least five proliferation genesets across five or more cancer types.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by analysis results shown in Figures 1E, 2D, and 2E. The high percentage of known lncRNAs validated in TCGA data provides strong evidence for the predictive accuracy of the approach, and the identification of 30 high-confidence uncharacterized lncRNAs represents a valuable resource for future studies.

results.result: Analysis of RNA-seq datasets from cells treated with DNA-damaging proliferation inhibitors or Nutlin-3 showed that proliferation/growth-suppressing lncRNAs were preferentially elevated and inducing lncRNAs were preferentially reduced, with reproducible patterns in p53 wild-type but not mutant cells, indicating crosstalk with p53-mediated tumor-suppressive pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 are supported by analysis of 14 RNA-seq datasets (7 DNA-damaging agents, 7 Nutlin-3) and 24 single-cell RNA-seq datasets, with results shown in Figures 3A and 3B. The consistency across multiple datasets and cell types, and the p53-dependence observed in single-cell data, provide strong evidence for the functional relevance of the identified lncRNAs.

results.result: The majority (59%) of lncRNAs showed differential expression in only one or two datasets supporting cell type-specific functions, while less than 5% were altered in more than five datasets.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 are supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and citation to Liu et al., 2017b. The distribution of lncRNA alterations across datasets is consistent with known cell type-specificity of lncRNA function and provides context for interpreting the meta-analysis results.

results.result: RobustRankAggreg meta-analysis identified 13 consistently upregulated lncRNAs (8 top proliferation/growth suppressors) and 4 consistently downregulated lncRNAs (3 top proliferation/growth inducers), including known examples like TMPO-AS1 (downregulated) and known p53-regulated tumor suppressors GUARDIN, PICART1, and LINC00475 (upregulated).
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 are supported by RobustRankAggreg meta-analysis results (BH adjusted p<0.05) shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary files. The identification of known examples among the top hits validates the meta-analysis approach, and the directional consistency (downregulation of inducers, upregulation of suppressors) supports the functional predictions.

results.result: The 13 consistently upregulated lncRNAs had significantly more p53-binding sites near their transcription start sites compared to background lncRNAs, including two poorly characterized lncRNAs PSLR-1 (FAM198B-AS1) and PSLR-2 (SEPTIN9-DT) that had consistently elevated expression upon p53 activation and p53-binding sites in at least nine ChIP-seq datasets.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 are supported by analysis of 17 p53 ChIP-seq datasets with Wilcoxon rank-sum test (p=1.65×10^-9) and RobustRankAggreg meta-analysis (BH adjusted p<5.48×10^-3), with results shown in Figures 2E, 3C, 3D, 3E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3. The convergence of expression and ChIP-seq evidence provides strong support for direct p53 regulation of these lncRNAs.

results.result: Experimental validation in A549 and H460 LUAD cell lines showed that PSLR-1 and PSLR-2 levels were significantly increased following exposure to four different p53-activating stimuli (Nutlin, etoposide, cisplatin, gamma radiation) compared to vehicle control.
results.evaluation: Claim C63 is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3F with appropriate positive (BAX) and negative (AchR) controls. The validation in an independent cell type (LUAD) not included in the meta-analysis datasets strengthens confidence in the generalizability of the findings. Statistical significance is reported for all conditions.

results.result: Both PSLR-1 and PSLR-2 were significantly reduced in LUAD patient samples compared to normal lung tissue.
results.evaluation: Claim C64 is supported by qRT-PCR data from patient samples (n=10 LUAD, n=5 normal) with t-test (p<1.23×10^-7) shown in Figure 4A. The downregulation in patient samples is consistent with loss of tumor-suppressive function during tumorigenesis and provides clinical relevance for the findings.

results.result: RNA-seq of A549 cells with elevated PSLR-1 or PSLR-2 expression showed significantly higher expression of genes with positive associations in TCGA LUAD, preferential elevation of tumor-suppressor genes and suppression of oncogenes, with significantly distinct distributions.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 are supported by RNA-seq data from lncRNA overexpression experiments with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests (p<7.9×10^-12 and p<5.6×10^-6) shown in Figures 4B and 4C. The consistency between TCGA associations and experimental perturbations provides strong validation of the computational predictions and demonstrates functional relevance.

results.result: GSEA of A549 cells with elevated PSLR expression showed the p53 pathway was consistently the top upregulated Hallmark geneset, while proliferation-linked genesets (E2F targets, G2M checkpoint, mitotic spindle, MYC targets) were consistently among the top downregulated pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69 are supported by GSEA results (FDR<0.05) shown in Figure 4D. The consistent ranking of p53 pathway upregulation and proliferation pathway downregulation across both PSLRs provides strong evidence for their tumor-suppressive functions and mechanistic insight into their mode of action.

results.result: Enrichr analysis showed E2F4 and FOXM1 were the most enriched transcriptional regulators for downregulated genes and p53 for upregulated genes with elevated PSLR expression, and HOMER analysis identified CHR (cell cycle genes homology region) motif as consistently enriched in promoters of downregulated genes, with literature evidence showing CHR-containing G2/M genes are activated by FOXM1-containing complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73 are supported by Enrichr and HOMER analyses shown in Figures 4E and 4F, with citation to Chen et al., 2013 and Sadasivam et al., 2012 for CHR function. The convergence of transcription factor enrichment, motif enrichment, and literature evidence provides strong mechanistic insight into how PSLRs regulate cell cycle genes.

results.result: Expression of PSLR-1 or PSLR-2 in A549 and H460 LUAD cells resulted in significantly decreased cell growth, decreased colony formation, and decreased live cell numbers without changes in viability, while MALAT1 overexpression increased cell growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are supported by MTT assays, colony formation assays, and Trypan Blue exclusion data shown in Figures 5A, 5B, 5C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, with appropriate statistical tests and replicates. The inclusion of MALAT1 as a positive control for proliferation-inducing lncRNA strengthens the interpretation. The consistency across multiple assays and two cell lines provides strong evidence for growth-suppressive functions.

results.result: Expression of PSLR-1 or PSLR-2 resulted in increased numbers of cells in G2/M phase, with phospho-histone H3 staining showing analogous percentages across conditions, indicating cells were arresting in G2 and not M phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are supported by flow cytometry cell cycle analysis and phospho-histone H3 staining shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, with appropriate positive control (colcemid). The discrimination between G2 and M arrest using phospho-histone H3 is methodologically sound and provides mechanistic insight into the growth-suppressive effects.

results.result: RNA-seq and validation experiments showed that elevated PSLR levels resulted in reduced expression of nine G2 regulatory genes and increased expression of three G2 regulatory genes, with changes observed at both RNA (qRT-PCR) and protein (Western blot) levels in A549 and H460 cells, consistent with G2 cell cycle arrest.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C84 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 6A), qRT-PCR data (Figure 6B), and Western blot data (Figure 6C) showing coordinated changes in G2 cell cycle regulators. The consistency across RNA and protein levels and across two cell lines provides strong evidence for the mechanism of G2 arrest. The median fold changes and FDR values reported for RNA-seq data are highly significant.

results.result: In TCGA patient samples across 10 cancer types, there was a significantly distinct expression distribution of genes that inhibit versus induce G2 cell cycle arrest when comparing samples with high versus low PSLR expression.
results.evaluation: Claim C85 is supported by Wilcoxon rank-sum tests (p=5.09×10^-4 for PSLR-1 and p=2.72×10^-4 for PSLR-2) shown in Figure 6D. The validation of G2 cell cycle gene expression patterns in patient samples provides clinical relevance and demonstrates that the experimental findings in cell lines are reflected in human tumors.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis showed that genes whose overexpression correlated with favorable patient outcome had preferentially higher expression with elevated PSLR levels, while genes linked to unfavorable prognosis were preferentially reduced, with significantly distinct distributions.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by RNA-seq data analysis with Wilcoxon rank-sum tests (p=1.54×10^-55 for PSLR-1 and p=2.49×10^-86 for PSLR-2) shown in Figure 7A. The extremely significant p-values and the directional consistency with prognostic associations provide strong evidence that PSLR levels impact patient-relevant gene expression programs.

results.result: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis showed that LUAD patients with high PSLR-1 or PSLR-2 expression had significantly increased overall survival compared to patients with low expression, with significant favorable prognostic associations also observed in multiple other cancer types.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90 are supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis with log-rank tests (p<7.0×10^-3 for LUAD) shown in Figure 7B. The survival associations across multiple cancer types provide strong clinical relevance for the findings and demonstrate that the growth-suppressive functions of PSLRs translate to patient outcomes.
